In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-A'la (The Most High).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾

The meaning of tasbih (glorification), which has already been explained, is declaring Allah free from everything that is unfitting. The command to glorify here is directed at "the name of your Lord." In other verses the command to glorify Allah Himself came, such as His saying: ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him and glorify Him for a long part of the night﴾ [al-Insan: 26], and like His saying: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17].

The glorification of the Lord, glorified is He, is like His saying: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat: 180]. Scholars differed regarding this verse: is the intended meaning the glorification of Allah, glorified is He, or the glorification of His name, exalted is He, as is the case here? Then they differed regarding the intended meaning of glorifying the name of Allah, exalted is He, and the question of the name and the named (al-ism wa'l-musamma) arose.

Al-Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) had already stated, in Surah al-Waqi'ah, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96], that the ba' (preposition) there enters upon the object, as it enters upon it in His saying: ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates﴾ [Maryam: 25]. He referred to an earlier discussion on this point, and he related the words of al-Qurtubi that the ism (name) means the musamma (the named). He cited in support from the speech of the Arabs the verse of Labid:

"Until the year is complete, then the name of peace upon you both; and whoever weeps a full year has made his excuse."

He said: In my view it is not necessary here that ism means musamma, since the intended meaning may be the name itself, because some people have deviated regarding the names of Allah, and others have declared them free from such deviation. Allah described them as being of utmost beauty, because they comprise His noble attributes, as in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. (p-499) And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra': 110]. Then he said: We do not wish to mention the speech of the theologians concerning the name and the named, whether the name is the named or not, because our purpose here is to explain the meaning of the verse. End quote.

His speech, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, thus contained the possibility that the intended meaning is declaring the name of Allah free from what the deviators have distorted it with, just as the possibility of declaring Allah free from everything unfitting to His majesty. It also contained that it is not necessary for ism here to mean musamma. We will, Allah willing, present a summary of explanation of these points.

As for declaring the names of Allah free (from impurity), it has several meanings, among them:

Declaring them free from being applied to idols, such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and the name of "the gods" (al-alihah).

Among them: declaring them free from being played with and made a subject of amusement, such as pronouncing them in a state that contradicts reverence and veneration, like one who toys and jests with them. Similar to this is one who is heedless and neglectful of his prayer: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4-5]. Or placing them in other than their proper places, such as engraving them on a garment or on a carpet that is used and trodden upon.

Among them: declaring them free from impure places. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he entered the toilet, would remove his ring, because it bore the engraving "Muhammad, Messenger of Allah" (ﷺ).

And from this: preserving written pages from being treated with contempt, out of honor for the name of Allah.

In light of this, this verse clarifies the verse of al-Waqi'ah, and that the name of your Lord occupies the position of the direct object, and that this is what is meant by glorification. And on the basis that the intended meaning is the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, they said: the ism is the musamma, as al-Qurtubi and others said, and they said: the ism is a complement (silah), as in the aforementioned verse of Labid.

As for the question of the ism: is it identical to the musamma or not? Al-Fakhr al-Razi pointed to it and said: it is a weak description (wasf rakik).

As for the Shaykh's statement (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him): "In my view it is not necessary here that ism means musamma," it requires a little elaboration to show the correctness of what he said.

(p-500) Al-Razi discussed it after an introduction, in which he said: Some people have held to this verse as evidence that the ism is the very musamma.

I say: Engaging in argument is not possible except after clarifying the point of dispute, so here it is necessary to explain what the ism is and what the musamma is.

We say: If by the ism is meant this utterance, and by the musamma is meant that essence, then no intelligent person can say "the ism is the musamma." If by the ism is meant that essence, and by the musamma likewise that essence, then our statement "the ism is the very musamma" means that this essence is that essence. No intelligent person can dispute this. So we know that this question, in its description, is weak. It was the homonymy of the word ism, which is the counterpart of the verb and the particle, that caused confusion among later scholars, since it is what the earlier scholars meant when they used it to refer to its named referent.

From here you know why the Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) turned away from explaining it. We have presented this brief explanation so that the reader may be acquainted with it. In any case, whether among the earlier or later scholars: if the possibility of such an issue arises concerning other beings, it does not arise concerning the essence of Allah and His names, because the names of Allah have rulings that do not apply to the names of others, and His names, glorified is He, have the right of glorification, declaration of their purity, and invocation by them, as has already been mentioned.

Here is a viewpoint that I have not seen anyone state explicitly, but it may be understood from the speech of some exegetes, and the Sunnah points to it: that the tasbih here means dhikr and worship, such as tahmid (saying al-hamdu lillah), tahlil (saying la ilaha illa Allah), and takbir (saying Allahu akbar).

In al-Razi's speech there is his statement: "The meaning would be: glorify your Lord by mentioning His names," and something similar appears in some of al-Tabari's reports.

As for the indication of the Sunnah to this, al-Tabari and others related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this verse was revealed, after reciting it he said (ﷺ): "Subhana Rabbiya al-A'la" (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High).

Likewise what is reported: when the verse ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74] was revealed, he (ﷺ) said: "Place it in your bowing (ruku')." And when this one was revealed, he said: "Place it in your prostration (sujud)."

(p-501) Al-Qurtubi related a lengthy report on its virtue in prayer and outside prayer, but it is not authentic.

And there came the authentic hadith: "And you praise Allah thirty-three times after each prayer, and glorify Him thirty-three times, and conclude the hundred with: la ilaha illa Allah."

It is authentically reported from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not pray any prayer after the revelation of: ﴿When the help of Allah comes and the victory﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], except that he would say: 'Subhanaka Rabbana wa bihamdika, Allahumma aghfir li,' " and she said: "He was interpreting the Qur'an."

Umm Salamah said: "He would say it while standing, sitting, coming and going (ﷺ), so that it became: 'Glorify the name of your Lord,' that is: mention your Lord."

This is what the other verse in this same surah indicates, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself, and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [al-A'la: 14-15]. It explicitly mentions remembrance of the name of your Lord, just as it came as ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾, so it placed remembrance in the position of glorification, which is what we have pointed to. And success is from Allah.

Allah's saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾.

He stated the creation absolutely so that it would encompass every created thing, as was mentioned earlier in "al-Sajdah" (Surah 32): ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7]. Al-taswiyah (proportioning) means al-taqwim (shaping in due form) and al-ta'dil (balancing). Allah has created every creature proportioned in the best manner suited to its nature and to the purpose for which it was created. He created the heavens and proportioned them in the strongest construction, the highest height, and the firmest cohesion, such that you see in them no rift or fissure, and He adorned them with the stars. He created the earth and spread it out, brought forth from it its water and its pasture, and set firm the mountains, making it a bed and a cradle. He created the trees and proportioned them to what suits them of fruit-bearing kinds and of fuel for fire, and other things besides.

Likewise, these animals in their creation and their proportioning are a sign: ﴿Do they not look at the camel, how it was created? And at the sky, how it was raised? And at the mountains, how they were set up? And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17-20].

As for man, he is in the best of forms. All of this necessitates that His name be glorified (p-502) in His essence and in all His attributes, since He combined creation and proportioning. This is due to the perfection of His power and His transcendence above every deficiency.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who measured [all things] and then guided [them]﴾.

He used the word "taqdir" (measuring, determining) without restriction, so that it would encompass every thing that is measured, and it refers to every created being, because among the necessary consequences of creation is taqdir, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, all things We have created with due measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49], and His saying: ﴿Allah has already set a measure for everything﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. This verse and its like are among the greatest signs of power. He, may He be exalted, gathered them together when giving the complete description of Allah, may He be exalted, when Pharaoh asked the Prophet of Allah, Musa, about his Lord, and he said: ﴿"Then who is your Lord, O Musa?" He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided [it]"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49-50].

The generality of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la: 2] has already been explained. Here He measured everything He created and guided every created being to what He had measured for it. So in the upper world He measured the measures of affairs and guided the angels to carry them out, and He measured the course of the celestial spheres and guided them to what was decreed for them: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾ [al-Anbiya': 33].

As for trees and plants, He measured for them specific times for their bearing fruit and their guidance to what was decreed for them: the root descends downward and the sprout grows upward. Likewise with animals in their mating, their offspring, and their nursing. Each has been guided to what was decreed for it, and likewise man.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: the whole world falls under the literal meaning of this verse.

As for its detailed meaning, it has preceded in the explanation of the Shaykh, may the mercy of Allah, may He be exalted, be upon us and upon him, in Surat Ta-Ha, at the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided [it]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

[p. 503]

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, has already explained the meaning of His saying, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ and ﴿except what Allah wills﴾. In his commentary on Surah Ta-Ha, in discussing His saying, ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], he said that "We will make you recite" means "We will make you recite" in Surah Ta-Ha. He clarified this with the verse in Surah al-Qiyamah: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16].

As for His saying, "so you will not forget," the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, examined it in order to remove the appearance of inconsistency together with the verses that are abrogated (naskh), so that he forgets them.

It will be printed, if Allah wills, together with this supplement, as a supplement to the benefit.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Surah al-A'la

His saying, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget, except what Allah wills﴾, and so on.

This noble verse indicates that the Prophet ﷺ forgets some of the Qur'an, that which Allah wills to make him forget. Many verses have come indicating the preservation of the Qur'an from being lost, such as His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16-17], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

The answer is that although the Qur'an is protected from being lost, some of it abrogates other parts. Allah's causing His Prophet to forget some of the Qur'an falls under the ruling of abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling or recitation by a later one). So when He makes him forget a verse, it is as if He abrogated it, and He must bring something better than it or its equal, as He stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring one better than it or the like thereof﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106].

And His saying: ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse, and Allah is most knowing of what He sends down﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], and so on.

Here He alluded, by His knowledge of the wisdom of abrogation, to His saying: ﴿Indeed, He knows what is declared and what is hidden﴾ [al-A'la: 7].

And His saying: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾.

This noble verse implies that reminding is only sought where there is a likelihood of benefit, as evidenced by the conditional particle "if" (in).

Many verses have come indicating the command to remind in an unrestricted manner, such as His saying: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 21], and His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 17].

Many answers have been given to this:

(p. 439) Among them: there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "if the reminder benefits, and if it does not benefit," like His saying: ﴿And garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold." This is the view of al-Farra', al-Nahhas, al-Jurjani, and others.

Among them: that "if" here means "when" (idh). Using "in" to mean "idh" is the position of the Kufans, contrary to the Basrans.

The Kufans took as examples of this His saying: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112], and His saying: ﴿And you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], and His saying: ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23], and His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

And His saying ﷺ: "And we, if Allah wills, will surely join you."

And the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*Do you get angry if the ears of Qutayba were cut off openly, yet you did not get angry at the killing of Ibn Hazim?*

The Basrans answered regarding the verses containing ﴿if you are believers﴾ that they contain the meaning of a condition, brought for the purpose of stirring up (emotion). Regarding the verse ﴿if Allah wills﴾ and the hadith, they said that these two are a teaching for servants on how to speak when they report about the future. And regarding the poem they gave two answers:

The first: it is from placing the cause in the position of the effect. The original meaning is: "Do you get angry if someone boasts of cutting off the ears of Qutayba," since boasting of that would be a cause of anger, and the consequence of the cutting.

The second: "Do you get angry if it becomes clear in the future that the ears of Qutayba were cut off?"

Among them: the meaning of ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ is guidance toward reminding about what is more important, i.e., remind about what is important and beneficial, rather than what has no benefit. Thus the meaning is: remind the disbelievers, for example, about the foundations, which are monotheism, not the branches, because the branches do not benefit without the foundations. And remind the believer who neglects an obligation, for example, about that neglected obligation, not about creedal matters and the like, because that is more beneficial.

Among them: that "in" means "qad" (indeed). This is the view of Qutrub.

(p. 440) Among them: that it is a conditional form intended to censure the disbelievers and to express the improbability of their remembering, as the poet said:

*You would have made them hear had you called a living one, but there is no life in those you call.*

Among them: other than that.

What appears clear to the one who specifies these letters, may Allah pardon him, is that the noble verse remains upon its apparent meaning, and that the Prophet ﷺ, after repeating the reminder to them repeatedly so that Allah's proof is established against His creation, is commanded to remind when there is a presumption of benefit. As for when he knows there is no benefit, he is not commanded to do something he knows has no benefit, because the intelligent person does not strive for what has no benefit.

The poet said:

*Strive, O wise one, for what is beneficial, so do not be one who strives for something whose benefit is far off through all time.*

This is clear, but the difficulty lies in realizing the ground of the ruling (tahqiq al-manat), and its clarification is that it should be asked: by what means is it certain that the reminder will not benefit, so that leaving it is permitted?

The explanation of that is that sometimes one knows it through Allah informing him of it, as happened with Abu Lahab, concerning whom Allah said: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame, and his wife, the carrier of firewood﴾ [al-Masad: 3-4].

So this Abu Lahab and his wife are not benefited by the reminder, because the Qur'an came down that they are among the people of the Fire, after repeated reminders to them, repeated to such a degree that Allah's proof was established against them. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ, after knowing this, is not obligated to remind them of anything, because of His saying in this verse: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾.

And sometimes one knows that by the evidence of the situation, such that he delivers the message in the most complete manner and brings clear miracles, and he knows that some persons know the truth of his prophethood but persist in disbelief out of obstinacy and stubbornness. Such a person does not require the reminder to be repeated to him forever, after it has been repeated upon him to the extent that the proof is established against him.

The summary of the clarification of this answer is that the reminder includes three wisdoms:

The first: the performer's release from the obligation of the command to it.

The second: the hope of benefit for the one who is admonished by it. Allah explained these two wisdoms by His saying: (p. 441) ﴿They will say, "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him"﴾ [al-A'raf: 164]. He explained the first of these by His saying: ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 54], and His saying: ﴿Upon you is only the delivery [of the message]﴾ [al-Shura: 48], and similar verses. He explained the second by His saying: ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55].

The third: the establishment of proof against the creation. He explained it by His saying: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165], and by His saying: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger"﴾ and so on [Ta-Ha: 134].

So when the Prophet ﷺ repeats the reminder, the first and third wisdoms are achieved. If there is hope in the second, he continues to remind; otherwise he is not obligated to continue. And knowledge is with Allah, the Most High.

We have chosen to keep the verse upon its apparent meaning, although most of the exegetes turn it away from its apparent, immediately understood meaning, which is: "So remind, in general, if the reminder benefits, and if it does not benefit." This is because we see that it is not permitted to turn the Book of Allah away from its apparent meanings that are understood from it, except by evidence that must be followed, and [we keep] this verse upon its apparent meaning.

Ibn Kathir inclined toward this in his explanation of it, saying: "That is, remind wherever the reminder is beneficial." From here is derived the etiquette of spreading knowledge: one does not place it in other than its people. As 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You will not speak to a people with a hadith that their minds cannot reach, except that it becomes a trial for some of them." He also said: "Speak to people with what they recognize. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?"

Note

This difficulty in this verse arises only according to the view of those who consider the argument from address (dalil al-khitab), which is the implicit meaning by contrast (mafhum al-mukhalafa). As for the view of those who do not consider mafhum al-mukhalafa a valid argument, whether as a condition or otherwise, such as Abu Hanifa, there is no difficulty in the verse. Likewise, there is no difficulty in it according to the view of those who do not consider the implicit meaning of a condition (mafhum al-shart), such as al-Baqillani. Then the verse explicitly commands reminding where there is a likelihood of benefit, and is silent about its ruling where there is no likelihood of benefit, so that it is sought from another proof. Thus the verse does not contradict the verses that indicate reminding in an unrestricted manner.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 9:

The Exalted said: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits.﴾

Is "in" (إنْ) here in the sense of "idh" (since, when), or is it conditional? And does the condition carry a implied contrary meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafa) or not? The Shaykh—may Allah the Exalted have mercy on us and on him—examined all of this at length, in order to remove the appearance of inconsistency. He preferred that it is conditional, and he divided the one being invited into three categories: one certain to benefit, one certain not to benefit, and one whose case is uncertain. He said: the place of reminding is where the person is not certain to be unbenefited, such as one who has been made clear to repeatedly and turned away, like Abu Lahab, about whom Allah has informed of his end, so there is no benefit in reminding him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already explained the wisdom behind reminding (al-dhikra).

Among its wisdoms is the reminding of the believers, and this was discussed in the commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remind, for reminding benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55], in surah "al-Dhariyat."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the most wretched will avoid it﴾ ﴿Who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾

That is: because of their wretchedness that preceded from eternity (azalan), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾ [Hud: 106].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾

He negated the two opposites, because a human being by his essence is either alive or dead, and there is no intermediate state between them. But on the Day of Resurrection the balances and the measures change, and this is more intense in punishment, for if he died he would find rest. Yet he suffers from the punishment what leaves no life with him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they should die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾ [Fatir: 36], and His saying: ﴿Death will come to him from every place, but he will not die﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, had already explained the meaning of this in Surat Ta-Ha, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 87, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly will succeed one who purifies himself﴾ ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾. Here He attributed success to ﴿one who purifies himself﴾ and ﴿remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾. In other than this verse, He attributed purification (tazkiyah) to the will of Allah, in His saying: ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been pure﴾ [An-Nur: 21]. In another verse, He forbade the purification of the self.

The Shaykh had already explained this in surah "An-Nur," when discussing His saying, ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been pure﴾, that "zaka" (became pure) means purified from ingratitude and sins, not that he paid zakah (alms). What appears to be the case is that the verse of "An-Najm" only forbade the purification of the self because it contains praise of oneself, and such praise may not be true, as in surah "Al-Hujurat": ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 14]. And Allah knows best.

It is the saying of the Most High: "Rather, you prefer the worldly life" (Qur'an 87:16), "while the Hereafter is better and more enduring" (87:17), "Indeed, this is in the former scriptures" (87:18), "the scriptures of Abraham and Moses" (87:19).

It has been read as "tu'thirūna" with the ta' and also with the ya' (yu'thirūna), referring back to "the most wretched" (al-ashqā) "who will enter the greatest Fire" (al-A'la 87:11-12). As for reading it with the ta' as address, it is more general. Since this matter is common among the past nations, and it is mentioned in all the former scriptures in general, and in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses in particular, this indicates its gravity and that it is a matter prevalent among people.

Verses have come indicating its causes, among them: ignorance and lack of knowledge of realities, as in His saying: "This worldly life is nothing but diversion and play. And indeed, the Abode of the Hereafter—that is the [eternal] life, if they only knew" (al-'Ankabut 29:64), i.e., the enduring life.

Al-Qurtubi related from Malik ibn Dinar his saying: "If the world were of gold that perishes, and the Hereafter were of clay that endures, it would be obligatory to prefer clay that endures over gold that perishes. How then, when the Hereafter is of gold that endures and the world is of clay that perishes?"

Among the causes of this is that the world has been beautified for people and hastened for them, as in His saying: (p-505) "Beautified for people is the love of desires: of women and sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilled land" (Al 'Imran 3:14).

Then He said: "That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, while with Allah is the best return" (Al 'Imran 3:14).

And Allah the Most High clarified this good return, which in its description corresponds to: "while the Hereafter is better and more enduring." He said: "Say, 'Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear Allah are gardens in the presence of their Lord, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally, and purified spouses, and approval from Allah. And Allah is Seeing of [His] servants'" (Al 'Imran 3:15).

Reflect upon this exchange: in the world there is gold, horses, women, cattle, and tilled land, and He answered all of that with the Garden, so it encompassed and included everything. But He specifically mentioned "purified spouses" so that the difference between the women of this world and the women of the Hereafter would be known, as was mentioned earlier: "rivers of honey purified, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of water not stale, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, [wherein] they will not be affected by intoxication, nor will they be exhausted" (al-Waqi'ah 56:19), and other things that explicitly state the superiority of the Hereafter.

There is no doubt that whoever prefers the Hereafter will prevail over whoever prefers the world and will be superior to him, as Allah the Most High explicitly stated in His saying: "The worldly life has been beautified for those who disbelieve, and they ridicule those who believe. But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah provides for whom He wills without account" (al-Baqarah 2:212).

From this it becomes apparent that the causes of people's preference for the worldly life are its beautification and adornment in their eyes: with wealth, sons, horses, and cattle: "Wealth and sons are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope" (al-Kahf 18:46).

This is cited not merely as a report of what exists, but behind it is what is called "lāzim al-fā'idah" (a necessary implication), which is the censure of one whose state is this, so it becomes obligatory to seek a remedy for this condition.

When we set out seeking the remedy, we are in fact confronting the most dangerous subject for a human being, since it encompasses his worldly life and his destination in the Hereafter, and it governs his happiness and success, or his wretchedness and deprivation. The nearest point of reference for us is precisely this place in this surah, together with what precedes it, His saying: "He who fears [Allah] will be reminded. But the most wretched will avoid it, who will burn in the greatest Fire" (al-A'la 87:10-12), and after it: "He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself, and remembers the name of his Lord and prays" (al-A'la 87:14-15). (p-506) These verses have divided the whole nation, the nation of the call, into two parts.

As for reminding and warning, when He said: "So remind, if the reminder benefits" (al-A'la 87:9), this is the position of the Prophet ﷺ. The division of the nation into the two parts came in the two verses: "He who fears [Allah] will be reminded," so he benefits from the reminder and it benefits him. "But the most wretched will avoid it," so it does not benefit him and he does not benefit from it. Then came the ruling of success: "He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself," meaning: he who fears [Allah], remembers the name of his Lord and prays, and does not neglect the remembrance of Allah the Most High. This very position is what is detailed in Surat al-Hadid, and in the context of guidance for us and reproach to the past nations as well: "Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah and what has been revealed of the truth, and that they not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and a long period passed over them so their hearts hardened, and many of them are defiantly disobedient?" (al-Hadid 57:16).

So hardness of heart, the lengthy passage of time, and procrastination are the fundamental factors of heedlessness and preference for the world. And fear and remembrance are the fundamental factors for preferring the Hereafter. Then He presented the world in its reality with His saying: "Know that the worldly life is but play and diversion and adornment and boasting among yourselves and competition in wealth and children—like the example of a rain..." up to His saying "And Allah is the possessor of great bounty" (al-Hadid 57:20-21).

Thus He described the disease and the remedy together in this context. The disease is delusion, and the remedy is racing toward forgiveness from Allah and His good pleasure.

As for His saying: "Indeed, this is in the former scriptures," it has been said: the demonstrative refers to the whole surah, because it includes the meanings of monotheism, the return (to Allah), the remembrance, and the acts of worship. "The former scriptures" are "the scriptures of Abraham and Moses," taken as an appositive (badal) of "the former."

It is found in al-Qurtubi that the scriptures of Abraham were parables, and the scriptures of Moses were admonitions, and he mentioned examples of them.

In al-Razi there is, "from the narration of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'How many books did Allah send down?' He said: 'One hundred and four books: upon Adam ten scrolls, upon Shith fifty scrolls, upon Idris thirty scrolls, upon Abraham ten scrolls, and the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan.'"

(p-507) In this there is a text that the Qur'an contains what is in the former scriptures, and there has come what indicates that other similar meanings are also in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, as in Surat al-Najm in His saying: "Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses, and of Abraham who fulfilled [his obligations]: that no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another, and that there is not for man except that for which he strives, and that his effort will be seen" (al-Najm 53:36-40).

This supports that most of them were parables and admonitions, and it also confirms the interconnection of the heavenly books.
